opus-5.5.text:
Sure. In pre-training, you're training the model to imitate all of the content on the internet, or on the web, including websites and code and so forth. So you get a model that can generate content that looks like random web pages from the internet. And the model is also trained to maximize likelihood, so it has to put a probability on everything. The objective is basically predicting the next token given the previous tokens. Tokens are like words, or parts of words. And since the model has to put a probability on it, and we're training to maximize log probability, it ends up being very calibrated. It can not only generate all of the content of the web, it can also assign probabilities to everything.

So the base model can effectively take on all of these different personas, or generate all these different kinds of content. Then when we do post-training, we're usually targeting a narrower range of behavior, where we basically want the model to behave like a kind of chat assistant. It's a more specific persona, where it's trying to be helpful. It's not trying to imitate a person; it's answering your questions or doing your tasks. And we're optimizing a different objective, which is more about producing outputs that humans will like and find useful, as opposed to just trying to imitate the raw content from the web.

So I'd say pre-training gives you the broad knowledge and capabilities, this huge distribution over everything, and post-training is about selecting out and shaping a particular behavior from that distribution, and making it reliable, so that you get something consistent that's actually useful to talk to.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training maximizes log probability and that this makes the model “very calibrated” and able to assign probabilities to everything.

r002.rationale: It describes the base model as having many personas and post-training as selecting and shaping a narrower chat-assistant behavior.

r003.rationale: It contrasts imitating raw web content during pre-training with optimizing post-training outputs for what people find useful.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that pre-training is basically teaching the model to imitate all the content on the internet, or at least a big chunk of it. So that's web pages, code, books, forum posts, whatever. And the objective is just to maximize likelihood, predict the next token. And what you end up with is a model that's really a kind of mixture over all the different people and sources that produced that text. It's not one coherent entity. If you give it the start of a Reddit thread, it'll continue like a Reddit commenter. If you give it the start of a paper, it'll continue like the authors of a paper. So it's a very capable model, it knows an enormous amount, but it doesn't have a fixed identity or a fixed set of goals. It's conditioning on context and then simulating whoever would plausibly have written that.

And then post-training is where you take that and narrow it down into a specific persona that's actually useful. In our case that's a chat assistant that's helpful, that's honest, that follows instructions, that says "I don't know" when it doesn't know rather than just continuing the text in the most plausible way. So you're selecting, out of this huge space of behaviors the pre-trained model can exhibit, one particular mode and reinforcing it. And the methods there are things like supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, and then RL from human feedback or other kinds of reward signals.

One thing I'd emphasize is that post-training is, in terms of compute, much smaller than pre-training. Most of the knowledge and most of the raw capability comes from pre-training. Post-training isn't really teaching the model a lot of new facts. It's more about shaping how the model uses what it already has. But I think people sometimes underrate how much it matters, because the difference between a base model and a well post-trained model in terms of actual usefulness is enormous. The base model is this kind of latent thing, and post-training is what makes it into a product you can talk to.

There's also a subtlety around calibration. The base model is actually pretty well calibrated in a sense, because the next-token objective rewards you for having the right probabilities. And some of what post-training does, if you're not careful, can mess that up. You can get the model to be overconfident or to hedge too much. So part of the art of post-training is getting the behavior you want without destroying the good properties that came from pre-training.

r001.rationale: The response says the next-token objective rewards correct probabilities and describes the base model as well calibrated.

r002.rationale: It characterizes post-training as selecting and reinforcing one assistant mode from the pretrained model’s broad range of behaviors.

r003.rationale: It contrasts pre-training’s imitation of internet content with post-training that shapes the model into a helpful, useful assistant.

astra-6.text:
I think of pre-training as giving the model a very broad repertoire of capabilities. It learns to predict text, and in doing that it learns a lot about the world, but also how to carry out computations, follow arguments, and imitate different kinds of behavior. It’s not necessarily trying to be a helpful assistant. Being a helpful assistant is just one kind of behavior that’s represented in the training data.

Post-training is where we take that repertoire and try to turn it into something you can actually interact with. We’re teaching it what to do when you ask a question: answer directly, follow your instructions, and use its capabilities in ways that are useful to you. So, to a first approximation, pre-training gives you the capabilities and post-training tells the model how to use them.

But I wouldn’t make that distinction too rigid. Post-training can also teach the model new things. If you train it with reinforcement learning on problems where it can check whether it got the right answer, it can learn better strategies for solving those problems. At that point, you’re doing more than just selecting a persona or changing the format of the response. You’re improving the underlying capability, too.

r001.rationale: The response says pre-training teaches the model to predict text and learn capabilities, but it does not state that maximizing log likelihood produces calibrated probability estimates.

r002.rationale: The response describes post-training as making the model useful to interact with, but does not clearly characterize it as narrowing a base model’s broad range of personas to an assistant persona.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts text prediction during pre-training with post-training for useful answers, but does not identify pre-training as imitating web content.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of pre-training as giving the model a very broad repertoire of behaviors and knowledge. It learns to predict text from lots of different sources, so it learns facts, patterns of reasoning, and how different kinds of people might respond in different situations. But that doesn’t by itself specify which of those behaviors you want when you ask it a question.

Post-training is where you try to turn that into a useful assistant. You’re teaching it to follow instructions, give answers that are helpful, and use its capabilities in the way you intended. So part of it is selecting among behaviors that the model already has.

But I wouldn’t draw a sharp line and say pre-training creates capabilities and post-training only elicits them. Post-training can also teach the model things, especially when you’re doing reinforcement learning on tasks where it can explore different approaches and get feedback. The distinction is more about the objective: predicting the text versus producing behavior that we actually want.

r001.rationale: The response describes pre-training as predicting text, but does not say that maximizing log likelihood produces calibrated probability estimates.

r002.rationale: It describes a broad repertoire of behaviors, then characterizes post-training as selecting among them to turn the model into a useful assistant.

r003.rationale: It contrasts text prediction with producing wanted behavior, but does not specifically identify pre-training as imitating web content.
